summary:
Busan stands under the national framework of South Korea. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. No source in the inventory documents a Busan-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern concerning trans people, so a visitor to this metropolitan city is assessed against the national picture.

The principal criminalising provision is the Military Criminal Act article 92-6, which penalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted, most visibly in the 2017 military operation that Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, in which 32 personnel were criminally charged and one gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su marks the sharpest documented harm of that exclusion. A military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap and she was compulsorily discharged in early 2020. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition exists and its surgical prerequisite has fallen away. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved registered-sex changes from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that determining gender change by surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery now serve as reference rather than criteria; the court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors. A 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register: an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, which Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 22 July 2024 an appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, holding that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change was approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction. At Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.
tangentialFactors:
Busan's own Pride history sits inside a national pattern of counter-protest violence. The 2018 Busan Pride deployment of roughly 2,000 police officers to shield 15,000 attendees is the local instance of the same dynamic that produced the Incheon attack by about 1,000 Christian protestors, after which organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society in South Korea alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people. The same organisation characterised the government's handling of NGO registration as years of bureaucratic obstruction, an appeal that continued after the Seoul Metropolitan Court judgment of March 2017.

Outing through official channels is a documented adjacent risk. The May 2020 Itaewon cluster showed contact tracing exposing LGBTQ people to doxing and online harassment, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street in the absence of a nondiscrimination bill.
localsOnly:
Residents face a legal gender recognition process that no longer requires surgery. The Yeongdong ruling of 8 May 2024 removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and reduced judicial guidelines demanding surgery to reference rather than criteria, and the Supreme Court's en banc decision of 24 November 2022 extended recognition to trans parents of minor children provided they are unmarried.

Transgender residents are excluded from military service, and those who serve risk the Military Criminal Act article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023 and carrying up to two years' imprisonment. The compulsory discharge of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su in early 2020, her death in March 2021, the Daejeon District Court's posthumous reinstatement of 7 October 2021 and the Defence Ministry's March 2024 line-of-duty recognition set the operative precedent.

Everyday protections are thin. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, same-sex couples cannot marry, enter a civil union or jointly adopt, and LGBTI organisations must still litigate for registration. Trans students report avoiding school restrooms, and the National Human Rights Commission of Korea's November 2023 finding of a hospitalisation blind spot followed the Ministry of Health and Welfare's refusal to draft guidelines for transgender patients.

Discrimination burden is measured at high levels: 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths harassed by classmates in a 2014 finding, 51.5% of transgender adults facing harsh discrimination in the past year in a 2018 study, and conversion therapy recommended to 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma. The 2025 survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults recorded pervasive discrimination at school, work and in transition-related care.
